did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the heading “For the director of music. Of David. A psalm,” presenting it as a psalm intended for performance and attributing it to David.
The expression “I waited patiently” emphasizes the psalmist’s prolonged and steadfast waiting for the Lord, until the Lord hears his cry.
The psalmist’s deliverance is portrayed as a move from a dangerous and unstable place—“the slimy pit” and “the mud and mire”—to “the rock,” where he can stand securely.
Deliverance gives rise to “a new song”: the psalmist’s personal transformation becomes a public testimony, so that many will see, fear, and trust in the Lord.
The chapter contrasts the person who trusts in the Lord with one who turns to “the proud” and “those who turn aside to falsehood”—expressions describing trust in pride, power, or lies.
The psalmist emphasizes that the number of the Lord’s wonders and his thoughts toward his people is so great that they cannot be fully arranged or counted.
In the verse “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire,” the focus shifts from outward ritual to listening and obedience: “but my ears you have opened.”
The expression “In the scroll of the book it is written about me” presents the psalmist’s coming and mission as part of what was written in the book, without specifying which book is meant.
The psalmist describes his desire to do God’s will, with the law as an inner reality: “Your law is within me.”

Despite the deliverance described at the beginning of the psalm, the conclusion returns to an urgent plea arising from poverty and distress; thus, the chapter connects thanksgiving for deliverance with a renewed prayer for help.
